source.title: The Inference-Compute Frontier for Limit Order Book Prediction

record.tranche_reason: Tests scaling-style loss-versus-inference-compute regularity and extrapolation in limit order book prediction, a new non-language setting.
record.gate_note: The paper tests held-out test cross-entropy against structural forward work and evaluates extrapolation to excluded MLPLOB operating points. The FastBiNLOB macro-F1 and latency results are not rows: they evaluate the paper's new architecture rather than the scaling relationship. The paper also reports a latency-axis fit, which is included as a contrast to structural work.
record.test_reason: In a new, non-language setting (FI-2010 limit order book prediction), the study fits L = L∞ + A·C^−α to the lower envelope of held-out test cross-entropy versus per-observation structural forward work. The fit uses heterogeneous low/mid-compute models and scores an excluded MLPLOB family 56×–2,515× beyond the fit range. This bears on whether the power-law form holds beyond text pretraining (V5). The compute axis is inference work across architecture families, not training compute, parameters or tokens within one family, so V1–V4 and V6 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that FI-2010 test cross-entropy has a finite empirical frontier in structural forward work, well summarized by a power law. The non-MLPLOB fit extrapolates to the excluded MLPLOB target frontier (R²=0.941), and the result is robust to 2× family-level work perturbations. Individual architectures such as W256 need not convert extra work into lower loss. Latency is a distinct, weaker coordinate, and the claims are empirical rather than general.
record.recipe_differences: Tests an inference-compute frontier for heterogeneous limit order book predictors, rather than language-model pretraining loss versus parameter count, training tokens, or training compute. Uses a finite lower envelope and an architecture-family holdout.
record.method_sensitivity: The fit varies by target subset and horizon; W256 performs worse than W64/W128. Structural work and measured latency produce different fit quality and reorder model families. Random family-level 2× work perturbations were also evaluated.
record.problems: Evidence is from one benchmark and a finite empirical frontier; the compute axis is a study-defined structural-work proxy rather than hardware instruction count. The paper acknowledges that the raw LOB40 scaling lane and full 144-feature deployment lane are not a direct feature-set comparison. The target-frontier extrapolation is strong, but all-target performance is weaker, particularly for dominated W256 targets.
record.rows_left_out: FastBiNLOB five-seed macro-F1 and latency results in Section 5 and Table 6 are omitted because they evaluate the proposed architecture, not the scaling relationship. Other latency percentiles and architecture timing summaries are likewise not separate scaling-law results.

untested.parts: Language-model pretraining loss vs parameters, tokens or training compute.
Extrapolation from small to much larger language-model training runs. The study's extrapolation is across architecture families on an inference-work axis.
Shape vs loss at fixed parameter count.
Downstream task performance vs scale or pretraining loss. The macro-F1 results evaluate FastBiNLOB, not a scaling relation.
Disagreement between published LM laws and compute-optimal splits. Horizon-dependent exponents and axis choice (work vs latency) are reported, but only within this non-LM V5 setting.

missing.what: Table 4 MAE, RMSE and within-0.05 fractions per target subset (e.g. W256 within-0.05 only 0.300 vs 0.900 for W128)

record.verdict_notes: The frontier is built from held-out test loss, and the 56 fit configurations were selected on CF1 validation lower envelopes, so this is a frontier description rather than a train-time prediction. The compute axis is per-observation inference work across heterogeneous families (trees, boosting, random-conv, MLPLOB), not training compute. I therefore linked all rows to V5 only, not V2 or V7. The reader's V7 'challenges' label was dropped: the perturbation check addresses fit robustness in a non-LM setting, not whether published LM laws disagree. The FastBiNLOB macro-F1 and latency results were correctly left out.

versions.untested_parts: The study is not about language-model held-out pretraining loss, parameter-count scaling, or token-count scaling.
Tests extrapolation across model families in FI-2010, not from small to large language-model training runs.
No fixed training-compute budget or loss-minimizing parameter/token allocation is studied.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Tests an inference-compute frontier for FI-2010 limit order book prediction, not image/video models, repeated data, fine-tuning, transfer, or the same training-loss relationship as text pretraining.
No downstream-task performance relationship to pretraining loss or language-model scale is tested.

Tests sensitivity to a particular structural-work counting convention using family-level multipliers. Does not test published language-model law disagreements, compute-optimal splits, or whether curves bend due to fitting method or training setup.

relationships.condition: FI-2010 raw LOB40, CF2–CF9 (and CF1-inclusive), structural-work axis, MLPLOB target frontier and W64/W128
relationships.reason: The non-MLPLOB power-law frontier predicts excluded MLPLOB losses 56×–2,515× beyond the fit range (r1, r3–r5, r11, r12). W64/W128 residuals are small (r7, r8). The in-sample full-envelope fit gives R²=0.902 (r13). The fit survives 2× family-level work perturbations (min R² 0.698) (r19). Fitted exponents are small (0.027–0.094) and vary by horizon (r14–r18).
relationships.display_finding: The frontier predicted excluded MLPLOB losses 56×–2,515× beyond the fitting range, with small W64/W128 residuals and in-sample full-envelope R² = 0.902; under 2× family-level work perturbations, minimum R² was 0.698, and exponents ranged from 0.027 to 0.094 across horizons.

relationships.condition: All operating points including dominated W256; CF1-inclusive all-target scoring; latency as compute axis
relationships.reason: W256 gets R²=0.647, with loss 0.493 vs implied 0.418, above W128 (r6, r9). All-target R² falls to 0.838, or 0.731 with CF1 (r2, r10). The regularity holds for the frontier, not within a family. Measured latency gives only R²=0.468 (r20).
relationships.display_finding: W256 loss was 0.493 versus 0.418 predicted, with R²=0.647 and worse loss than W128; all-target R² was 0.838, falling to 0.731 with CF1; the regularity held along the frontier rather than within model families, and measured latency yielded R²=0.468.
